text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Safety warning: a 20 kW standby set that stalls under building load after 15 minutes can drop transfer power unexpectedly, and repeated hot-restart attempts can overheat the starter, battery cables, and exhaust-side components; suspend summer peak-load testing until fuel-pressure and shutdown-circuit checks are completed.
- Most likely root cause is heat-related fuel delivery loss at the electric lift pump or its control circuit, causing low supply pressure to the high-pressure/common-rail system once under sustained load; confidence 68%.
- The physical mechanism fits the 15-minute pattern: as generator compartment temperature rises, the lift pump armature windings, commutator, or internal check valve lose efficiency, or a heat-soaked relay/connector increases resistance; fuel pressure then falls below Cummins control thresholds under load, combustion leans out, engine speed decays, and the controller commands shutdown or the engine simply dies. After about 30 minutes of cooling, winding resistance drops, the pump spins again, and the set restarts normally.
- The code text ECU-1425 is important even though no auto-detected code list was captured. On Cummins/PowerCommand systems, ECU-prefixed faults in this range commonly point to an engine-side electronic fault or shutdown condition rather than a simple maintenance reminder. The exact SPN/FMI mapping must be confirmed from the RS20A controller event log, but the presence of ECU-1425 strengthens the case for an electronically monitored fuel or protection event rather than a purely mechanical seizure.
- The symptom only appearing during summer peak tests is a major clue. Ambient heat plus enclosure recirculation raises fuel temperature, pump temperature, and connector resistance faster than winter exercise cycles. A restricted fuel path can pass a no-load weekly exercise but fail at 60-100% load after 10-20 minutes.
- Age matters on a 2016 RS20A. At roughly 8-10 years, electric fuel pumps, relays, and weather-exposed terminals are in the common failure window even when oil level is correct, vents are clear, and the fuel filter was changed last season.
- Data Needed
- Fuel supply pressure at cold start, at 10 minutes, and at stall, recorded in psi or kPa.
- Controller event log screenshot showing the full text behind ECU-1425, plus any shutdown reason such as low fuel pressure, overspeed, high coolant temp, or low oil pressure.
- Infrared temperature readings on the lift pump body, fuel rail supply line, coolant outlet, and enclosure air near stall time.
- Battery voltage at the pump feed and relay output during the last 60 seconds before stall.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Second-ranked cause is a false thermal shutdown from a drifting coolant temperature sender, high-engine-temp switch, or wiring fault, confidence 22%. The mechanism is sensor resistance drifting upward as temperature rises, making the ECU or PowerCommand controller interpret normal operating temperature as an overtemp event. That would explain a repeatable hot shutdown and restart after cooling. It ranks below the fuel hypothesis because the customer already confirmed cooling vents are clear, and there is no mention of boil-over, fan noise change, or a clear high-temp code.
- Third-ranked cause is ignition/actuator power loss from a heat-sensitive control relay, ECU power feed, or harness connection, confidence 10%. The mechanism is thermal expansion at a relay contact or oxidized terminal increasing voltage drop until the ECU, fuel shutoff actuator, or pump loses power under vibration and load. This also explains a cool-down restart. It ranks below the first two because the load-related timing points more strongly to fuel demand increasing with heat, and because many relay faults are less tightly tied to a 15-minute thermal soak.
- Equipment-specific pattern on Cummins residential/light-commercial standby sets from the mid-2010s is that “runs fine cold, dies hot, restarts later” is more often fuel-supply or shutdown-signal related than internal engine damage. The absence of low-oil symptoms and the correct oil level reduce the likelihood of a lubrication-triggered stop.
- A partially restricted fuel pickup, tank vent, or collapsing suction hose remains a sub-variant of the primary fuel diagnosis rather than a separate top-three cause. It can mimic a weak pump by creating increasing vacuum as fuel demand rises under summer load.
- Less likely causes include failing ignition coils on gaseous units, but the RS20A designation is commonly diesel-configured in field references; because the customer mentioned a fuel filter change, the fuel-supply path remains the more coherent fit.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test 1: pull the full controller and engine ECU event history with Cummins INSITE or the RS20A/PowerCommand service interface, including timestamped shutdown reason and freeze-frame values. Tool: Cummins INSITE laptop or dealer service tool. Expected result for the primary cause is a logged low-fuel-pressure, engine derate, or unexplained engine stop coinciding with rising temperature and load. A logged high coolant temperature with normal fuel pressure points to the secondary cause. Typical cost: $125-$225.
- Test 2: install a mechanical or electronic fuel-pressure gauge at the lift-pump outlet or specified test port and monitor pressure from cold start through 20 minutes at 50-100% load bank. Tool: 0-30 psi gauge or transducer, hoses rated for diesel, load bank. Expected result for the primary cause is pressure dropping as temperature rises, often from normal cold pressure into a low-pressure stall zone just before shutdown. Stable pressure with shutdown points away from the pump and toward thermal protection or electrical loss. Typical cost: $180-$350.
- Test 3: voltage-drop test on the lift-pump feed, pump ground, and pump relay under load at minute 1 and minute 14. Tool: DVOM with min/max capture. Expected result for the primary cause is either low delivered voltage under heat, such as more than 0.5 V drop on the feed or more than 0.2 V on the ground, or normal voltage with falling pressure indicating internal pump failure. If voltage disappears entirely at stall, the tertiary relay/harness cause moves up. Typical cost: $90-$180.
- Test 4: compare live coolant temperature from ECU data to an infrared thermometer or contact thermocouple at the thermostat housing. Tool: scan data plus IR gun. Expected result for the secondary cause is ECU temperature reading materially higher than actual metal temperature, or a shutdown switch opening below spec. If actual coolant is normal, a false overtemp is confirmed. Typical cost: $75-$150.
- Test 5: temporary bypass/known-good substitution of the fuel pump relay and inspection of heat-discolored connectors at the pump, relay base, and ECU power feed. Tool: relay tester or known-good relay, terminal tension tools. Expected result for the tertiary cause is immediate correction with relay substitution or visible terminal heat damage. Typical cost: $60-$140.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Ask: “Can you show me the complete event log behind ECU-1425, including the shutdown reason and freeze-frame values?” They should provide a printout or screen capture with coolant temp, battery voltage, engine speed, and any fuel-pressure-related data. Red flag: “The code isn’t important” or “We cleared it already.”
- Ask: “What was fuel supply pressure cold, at 10 minutes, and at the exact stall point under load?” They should give actual psi or kPa numbers and identify the test port used. Red flag: “We didn’t need a gauge because the filter is new.”
- Ask: “What voltage did the lift pump receive under load, and what was the voltage drop across the relay and ground?” They should show DVOM readings with min/max capture. Red flag: “Battery voltage was fine” without circuit-specific numbers.
- Ask: “Did you compare ECU coolant temperature to an external thermometer at the thermostat housing?” They should show both readings in °F or °C. Red flag: “The vents were clear so it can’t be temperature-related.”
- Ask: “Did you run it on a load bank until failure, or only idle/exercise mode?” They should state the kW load and run time. Red flag: any diagnosis made without reproducing the 15-minute loaded stall.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “I’ve done some research and want to understand how you verified the shutdown on this 2016 Cummins RS20A under load, especially the ECU-1425 event and fuel-pressure behavior.”
- Phrasing: use curiosity language such as “Can you walk me through the readings?” instead of “You didn’t test it right.” That keeps the discussion on data like psi, volts, and °F rather than ego.
- Example dialogue: “I’ve done some research and want to understand what ECU-1425 translated to on your scan tool.” “What was the fuel supply pressure at cold start and right before stall?” “Did the pump keep full battery voltage when hot?” “How did actual coolant temperature compare with the ECU reading?” “What load-bank percentage did you use to reproduce the failure?”
- Body language: bring a notebook, stand beside the technician if allowed, and write down exact values like 12.4 V, 8 psi, or 228 °F. Calm note-taking signals that you expect measurable proof.
- Response handling: if they get defensive, say, “I’m not challenging your experience; I’m trying to approve the right repair the first time, and these readings help me do that.” That phrase redirects the conversation to avoiding unnecessary parts.
- Exit strategy: “I appreciate your time. I’d like the event-log printout and test readings before authorizing parts.” If they still resist, say, “I’m going to pause here and get another shop to duplicate the loaded stall with pressure and voltage data.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says...” or “I got a second opinion online.”
- ALWAYS say: “I’ve done some research and want to understand...”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Fair diagnostic cost for this case is $250-$550 total if the shop performs event-log retrieval, loaded fuel-pressure testing, voltage-drop testing, and temperature correlation. Anything under $100 usually means they did not reproduce the 15-minute loaded failure.
- If the primary cause is a failed electric lift pump, fair parts pricing is commonly $180-$450 for the pump assembly depending on Cummins Onan packaging, plus $20-$60 for a relay, $15-$40 for terminals, and $25-$70 for hoses or clamps if heat-damaged. Exact RS20A part number must be confirmed by spec letter and serial number.
- Labor for pump replacement and retest is typically 1.5-3.0 hours on a standby enclosure, with another 0.5-1.0 hour for load-bank confirmation. At $125-$185 per labor hour, labor should land around $250-$740.
- A realistic total for diagnosis plus primary repair is $700-$1,700 depending on access, enclosure layout, and whether the shop includes a 30-minute loaded verification run.
- Overcharge markers are a $2,000-plus estimate without pressure data, charging separately for multiple “guess” parts like sensor, relay, and pump before testing, or billing 4.0-plus hours for a simple relay/pump swap without corrosion repair evidence.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts-cannon behavior on this symptom usually means replacing the fuel filter again, then the battery, then the starter, then a generic temperature sensor without ever recording fuel pressure at stall. A new filter from last season does not rule out pump failure, but it does make blind filter replacement a weak first move.
- Watch for diagnostic shortcuts such as a five-minute idle test, clearing ECU-1425 without printing it, or declaring “overheating” because the shutdown happens in summer. A true diagnosis must reproduce the fault under load for at least 15-20 minutes.
- Price gouging red flags include charging OEM ECU prices for a relay-level problem, quoting a full injector or high-pressure pump job before checking low-side supply pressure, or refusing to return replaced parts like the pump or relay for inspection.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: paid diagnostics that include event-log extraction, loaded fuel-pressure monitoring, voltage-drop testing at the pump circuit, and coolant-temperature correlation with an external thermometer.
- Reject outright: any recommendation for injector replacement, ECU replacement, or “complete fuel-system overhaul” made before the shop shows pressure readings, voltage readings, and the full meaning of ECU-1425.
- Get a second opinion if the shop cannot reproduce the stall on a load bank, cannot provide actual psi/volt/°F numbers, or insists the issue is “probably heat” without identifying whether the heat affects fuel delivery, sensor input, or power supply.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- On a Cummins RS20A, the engine must hold stable speed under load so the alternator can maintain 60 Hz output. To do that, the ECU depends on adequate low-side fuel supply, accurate temperature input, and uninterrupted electrical power to the pump and control circuits.
- In the primary failure mode, the lift pump is the weak link. Cold fuel and a cool pump allow normal pressure at startup. As enclosure temperature rises during a 15-minute summer load test, internal pump resistance increases and output volume falls. Under no-load exercise, the engine may still survive because fuel demand is lower; under building load, the same weak pump cannot keep up.
- Once supply pressure drops, the injection system receives less fuel than commanded. Combustion energy falls, engine rpm sags, and the controller may log an engine-side fault such as ECU-1425 before shutdown. After a 30-minute cool-down, the pump regains enough efficiency to restart, which is why the symptom repeats so consistently.
- In the secondary failure mode, the engine may not actually be overheating. A drifting sender can falsely report 230-250 °F when the thermostat housing is materially cooler. The controller then protects the engine by shutting it down even though airflow and coolant flow are acceptable.
- Prevention for this exact pattern means annual loaded testing with recorded fuel pressure and coolant temperature, not just weekly no-load exercise. Heat-related faults hide during easy runs and only appear when the set is asked to deliver rated kW in summer conditions.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Because this is a Cummins RS20A, exact part numbers depend on the genset spec letter and serial number, which were not provided. The shop should identify the model/spec from the nameplate before ordering any pump, relay, or sender.
- For the lift pump and shutdown-related sensors, OEM Cummins Onan parts are preferred because connector indexing, pressure calibration, and duty-cycle durability matter on standby equipment that may sit for weeks and then run at full load. Cheap aftermarket pumps often match bolt pattern but not hot-fuel flow rate.
- Good pricing sources are Cummins QuickServe for part identification, Cummins-authorized dealers for current supersessions, and reputable industrial suppliers cross-referencing Bosch/TI Automotive components where applicable. Ask for the old and new part numbers if a supersession exists.
- Relays and terminals can sometimes be sourced from TE Connectivity, Delphi/Aptiv, or Littelfuse equivalents if the shop matches amperage, terminal plating, and cavity fit exactly. For the pump itself, OEM is the safer choice.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor the discussion with the fair diagnostic and repair range: “If this is a lift-pump or pump-circuit heat failure, I understand diagnosis plus repair is usually about $700 to $1,700 including a loaded retest.” That number keeps the estimate tied to realistic labor and parts.
- Ask labor-justification questions: “How many hours are for diagnosis versus replacement?” “How many hours are for enclosure access?” “Is the final 30-minute load-bank verification included?” Shops that can explain 2.0 hours versus 4.5 hours are usually billing honestly.
- Use data as leverage: if they cannot show fuel pressure at stall, ask them to cap authorization at diagnostics only. If they can show pressure collapse with full pump voltage, approving the pump is reasonable; if they cannot, do not fund guesswork.
- Walk away if they quote ECU replacement first, refuse to decode ECU-1425, or stack multiple speculative parts on one estimate. Your leverage is that another Cummins-capable shop can verify this fault with a gauge and scan tool in one visit.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: heat-related low fuel supply pressure from a failing electric lift pump, restricted suction path, or pump control circuit, 68% confidence. The repeatable 15-minute loaded stall, 30-minute cool restart, summer-only trigger, and engine-side ECU-1425 event fit a thermal fuel-delivery collapse better than internal engine damage.
- Secondary cause: false high-temperature shutdown from a drifting coolant temperature sender, shutdown switch, or related wiring, 22% confidence. The hot-only shutdown and cool restart fit, but clear vents and lack of a clearly identified overtemp code keep it below the fuel hypothesis until temperature correlation is tested.
- Tertiary cause: heat-sensitive relay, connector, or ECU power-feed interruption affecting the pump or shutdown circuit, 10% confidence. This can mimic both other faults, especially if voltage disappears only when hot, but it is less specifically tied to load demand than a weak fuel pump.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate action: do not continue unattended summer peak tests until the set is load-tested with a fuel-pressure gauge and event-log capture. Repeated hot stalls can leave the transfer switch without expected backup power and can carbon-load the engine from repeated restart attempts.
- Near-term service plan: have a Cummins-capable shop perform annual loaded testing at 50-100% rated kW for at least 30 minutes, with recorded fuel pressure, battery voltage, and coolant temperature. On an approximately 2016 unit, add connector inspection and relay-base terminal tension checks to the yearly PM.
- Warning signs to monitor now are longer crank time after heat soak, slight hunting before stall, a sharper drop in exhaust note just before shutdown, or any recurrence of ECU-1425. Those details help distinguish pressure loss from a clean sensor-triggered shutdown.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Cummins QuickServe Online, service literature and parts lookup for generator engine diagnostics and fault interpretation: https://quickserve.cummins.com
- Cummins Onan generator manuals and service publications portal, used to identify RS-series controller procedures and shutdown diagnostics by model/spec: https://www.cummins.com/generators/manuals
- Smokstak Onan/Cummins generator technical forum, field-documented hot-stall and fuel-pump failure patterns on standby sets, useful as independent corroboration after OEM literature: https://www.smokstak.com/forum/forums/onan-cummins-kohler-generac-and-cat-generator-forums.1/
- Ask the servicing dealer specifically for the RS20A model/spec service manual section covering shutdown fault history, fuel-pressure test procedure, and coolant-temperature sensor resistance checks, plus any Cummins service advisories superseding the original lift pump or relay part number.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize only data-driven diagnostics: event-log retrieval for ECU-1425, loaded fuel-pressure testing, pump-circuit voltage-drop testing, and coolant-temperature correlation.
- If fuel pressure falls as the unit heats up, approve lift-pump/circuit repair and require a 30-minute load-bank retest before pickup.
- If the shop cannot provide actual psi, volts, and °F readings, stop authorization and move the generator to a Cummins-capable shop for a second opinion.
